label: inner+product+adjoint
title: Proof
body_md:
We will first prove that (\ref{formal+kernel}) holds. For $k=0$, $[q^0](1-q)\mathcal G_{a,b}(q)=1$ and it follows from $V_{b,0}=\mathbb Q x_0^b$ and $\mathcal D x_0^b=0$ that
the dimension of the kernel is one. So (\ref{formal+kernel}) is obvious for $k=0$. In the following it suffices to prove that
$\mathcal D:V_{b,k}\to V_{b,k-1}$ is surjective for
$1\le k\le ab/2$. Indeed, combining surjectivity and
\eqref{eq:kernel-dimension} yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dim\ker\mathcal D
 &=\dim V_{b,k}-\dim V_{b,k-1}\\
 &=[q^k]\mathcal G_{a,b}(q)-[q^{k-1}]\mathcal G_{a,b}(q)\\
 &=[q^k](1-q)\mathcal G_{a,b}(q).
 \end{aligned}
\]


We now present the proof of the required surjectivity. In the following proof,
we extend the domain $\mathbb Q[x_0,\ldots,x_a]$ of $\mathcal D,\mathcal E,\mathcal H$ and $V_{b,k}$ onto $\mathbb R[x_0,\ldots,x_a]$.
Since the corresponding matrix of the linear operator $\mathcal D$ acting on monomial bases has rational entries, this extension does not change its
rank and kernel dimension. Thus surjectivity and the dimension of its kernel are unaffected by this
change of scalars.

For any $\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in V_{b,k}$ and $\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in V_{b,k}$, define a bilinear inner product by
\[
 \langle \textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rangle
 :=\begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\left(\prod_{i=0}^{a}\alpha_i!\right)
   \prod_{i=0}^{a}\left(\frac{i!(a-i)!}{a!}\right)^{\alpha_i},
   &\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\boldsymbol{\beta},\\
 0,&\boldsymbol{\alpha}\ne\boldsymbol{\beta}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Obviously, this inner product is nonnegative.
We write $\|f\|^2=\langle f,f\rangle$.
We first give the next claim.

\begin{cla} The inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ on $V_{b,k}$ makes $\mathcal E$ adjoint to $\mathcal D$, i.e.,
\begin{eqnarray}\label{inner+product+adjoint}
\langle\mathcal D f,g\rangle=\langle f,\mathcal E g\rangle
\end{eqnarray}
for all $f,g$ in $V_{b,k}$. 
\end{cla}

\begin{proof}
To obtain this identity, we will assign positive
weights to the monomial basis. Let $\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in V_{b,k}$ be an arbitrary monomial with $\alpha_i>0$
for $1\le i\le a$. And assume that
$\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\boldsymbol{e}_i+\boldsymbol{e}_{i-1}$, where $\boldsymbol{e}_i$ is the coordinate
vector corresponding to $x_i$. Then in terms of the definition of the inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, we obtain
\begin{eqnarray}\label{form+two+vectors}
\frac{\|\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\|^2}{\|\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\|^2}
 =\frac{\alpha_{i-1}+1}{\alpha_i}\frac{a-i+1}{i},
\end{eqnarray}
In addition, it follows from the definitions of the operator $\mathcal D$ and the inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ that
\begin{eqnarray}
\langle\mathcal D \textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rangle
 &=&i\,\alpha_i\,\|\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\|^2,\label{inner+product+adjoint+1}\\
 \langle \textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\mathcal E \textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rangle
 &=&(a-i+1)(\alpha_{i-1}+1)\,\|\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\|^2.\label{inner+product+adjoint+2}
\end{eqnarray}
Thus, by (\ref{form+two+vectors})-(\ref{inner+product+adjoint+2}), we obtain
\begin{eqnarray}
\langle\mathcal D \textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rangle
 &=& \langle \textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\mathcal E \textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\rangle
\end{eqnarray}
for any $\textbf{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in V_{b,k}$ with all $\alpha_i>0$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\boldsymbol{e}_j+\boldsymbol{e}_{j-1}$, where $\boldsymbol{e}_j$ is the coordinate
vector corresponding to $x_j$. In addition, for any pair of monomials not related in this way, their inner
product is zero. Therefore, using the bilinearity of the inner product gives the identity (\ref{inner+product+adjoint}) for all $f,g$ in $V_{b,k}$. This prove this claim.
\end{proof}


Fix $1\le k\le ab/2$. Let $y\in V_{b,k-1}$ be orthogonal
to the image of $\mathcal D:V_{b,k}\to V_{b,k-1}$.
For every $x\in V_{b,k}$, adjointness (\ref{inner+product+adjoint}) gives
$\langle x,\mathcal E y\rangle=\langle\mathcal D x,y\rangle=0$.
Since $\mathcal E y\in V_{b,k}$, taking $x=\mathcal E y$
                                                                                                                                 
we have
$\langle\mathcal D\mathcal E y,y\rangle=0$.
On the other hand, using $\mathcal D\mathcal E-\mathcal E\mathcal D=\mathcal H$,
$\mathcal H y=(ab-2k+2)y$, and adjointness, we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \langle\mathcal D\mathcal E y,y\rangle
  &=\langle(\mathcal E\mathcal D +\mathcal H) y,y\rangle\\
  &=\langle\mathcal E\mathcal D y,y\rangle
    +\langle\mathcal H y,y\rangle\\
                                              
                                    
  &=\langle\mathcal D y,\mathcal D y\rangle
    +\langle(ab-2k+2)y,y\rangle\\
  &=\|\mathcal D y\|^2+(ab-2k+2)\|y\|^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
In consequence, we derive $\|\mathcal D y\|^2+(ab-2k+2)\|y\|^2=0$.
Here $ab-2k+2\ge2$. Thus, in terms of the nonnegativity of the inner product, we have $\|y\|^2=0$, which further implies $y=0$.
Thus $(\operatorname{im}\mathcal D)^\perp=\{0\}$ in $V_{b,k-1}$.
Since $V_{b,k-1}$ is finite-dimensional,
$\operatorname{im}\mathcal D=V_{b,k-1}$, so $\mathcal D$ is surjective.

Finally, in order to prove that the coefficient sequence of
$\mathcal G_{a,b}$ is unimodal, by \eqref{eq:kernel-reciprocity}, it suffices
to show that the coefficients are nondecreasing up to $ab/2$, which is immediate from the nonnegativity of $[q^k](1-q)\mathcal G_{a,b}(q)$ for $1\le k\le ab/2$ in the kernel formula (\ref{formal+kernel}). This completes the proof of this lemma.

label: gass:A-1+B-1
title: Proof
body_md:
By (\ref{def+Gauss+poly}) of Gaussian polynomials, we have
\begin{equation}\label{gass:A-1+B-1}
{A-1\brackB-1}
  =\frac{N(q)}
         {D(q)},
\end{equation}
where
\[
N(q):=\prod_{j=A-B+1}^{A-1}(1-q^j),
\quad
D(q):=\prod_{j=1}^{B-1}(1-q^j).
\]
We will evaluate this quotient (\ref{gass:A-1+B-1}) by separating the factors that vanish at $\zeta$.
Since \(\zeta\) is a primitive \(r\)-th root of unity, we have
\[
\zeta^j=1
\iff
r\mid j.
\]
Thus a factor \(1-q^j\) vanishes at \(q=\zeta\) exactly when \(r\mid j\), and every such zero is simple because
\[
\frac{d}{dq}(1-q^j)\Big|_{q\rightarrow\zeta}
=
-j\zeta^{j-1}\neq 0.
\]

For a set, let
$
Z(I):=|\{j\in I:\ r\mid j\}|
$
denote the number of multiples of \(r\) in \(I\).
We also let $B=k\,r$ since \(r\mid B\). For the denominator $D(q)$, we have
\[
Z([1,B-1])=k-1.
\]
 Hence \(D(q)\) has a zero \(q=\zeta\) of order \(k-1\). For the numerator $N(q)$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{number+zeros:A-1+B-1}
Z([A-B+1,A-1])
=
\left\lfloor \frac{A-1}{r}\right\rfloor
-
\left\lfloor \frac{A-B}{r}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor \frac{A-1}{r}\right\rfloor
-
\left\lfloor \frac{A}{r}\right\rfloor
+
k.
\end{equation}


We now split into the following two cases to consider:

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 1: \(r\nmid A\).}
Then
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{A-1}{r}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor \frac{A}{r}\right\rfloor,
\]
so
\[
Z([A-B+1,A-1])=k.
\]
Thus  $N(q)$ has one more zero \(q=\zeta\) than $D(q)$. Hence
we obtain
\begin{equation}
\left.{A-1\brackB-1}\right|_{q\rightarrow\zeta}=\left.\frac{N(q)}{D(q)}\right|_{q\rightarrow\zeta}=0.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 2: \(r\mid A\).} Let $A=\ell\, r$. Obviously, $\ell\geq k\geq1$ since $A\geq B$.
Then
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{A-1}{r}\right\rfloor
=
\ell-1,
\quad
\left\lfloor \frac{A}{r}\right\rfloor
=
\ell.
\]
Therefore,  (\ref{number+zeros:A-1+B-1}) gives
\[
Z([A-B+1,A-1])
=
\ell-1-\ell+k
=
k-1.
\]
So the numerator $N(q)$ and denominator $D(q)$ have the zero \(q=\zeta\) of the same order $k-1$.

The nonvanishing factors in $N(q)$ are those with \(r\nmid j\). In the interval
\[
A-B+1\le j\le A-1,
\]
there are \(B-1=k\,r-1\) indices, among which \(k-1\) are multiples of \(r\). Hence each nonzero residue class modulo \(r\) occurs exactly \(k\) times. For the
denominator, it is the same as the numerator. Therefore the products of the nonvanishing factors in \(N(q)\) and \(D(q)\) have the same value at \(q=\zeta\), and their ratio is \(1\).

It remains to compare the vanishing factors. The multiples of \(r\) in $N(q)$ correspond to
\[
j=r\, m,
\quad
m=l-k+1,l-k+2,\dots,l-1.
\]
The multiples of \(r\) in $D(q)$ correspond to
$
j=r\, m,\,
m=1,2,\dots,k-1.
$
Thus, we obtain
\begin{eqnarray*}
\left.\frac{N(q)}{D(q)}\right|_{q\rightarrow\zeta}
&=&\lim_{q\to \zeta}
\frac{
\prod_{m=l-k+1}^{l-1}(1-q^{rm})
}{
\prod_{m=1}^{k-1}(1-q^{rm})
}\\
&
=&\lim_{q\to \zeta}
\frac{
\prod_{m=l-k+1}^{l-1}(1-q^r)\left(1+q^r+q^{2r}+\cdots+q^{(m-1)r}\right)
}{
\prod_{m=1}^{k-1}(1-q^r)\left(1+q^r+q^{2r}+\cdots+q^{(m-1)r}\right)
}\\
&=&\frac{
\prod_{m=l-k+1}^{l-1} m
}{
\prod_{m=1}^{k-1} m
}\\
&
=&\binom{l-1}{k-1}.
\end{eqnarray*}

Substituting \(l=A/r\) and \(k=B/r\), we get
\[
\left.
\begin{bmatrix}
A-1\\
B-1
\end{bmatrix}\right|_{q\rightarrow \zeta}
=
\binom{A/r-1}{B/r-1}.
\]

Combining both two cases yields the proof of this lemma.

label: eq:P+zata
title: Proof
body_md:
(i)
Set
$
N(q)=P(q)-[n+1]_q R(q).
$
We first show that \(N(q)\) vanishes at every root of \([m]_q\). Let \(\zeta\) be a root of \([m]_q\). Then \(\zeta\) is a primitive \(c\)-th root of unity for some integer \(c>1\) with \(c\mid m\).

We first compute $P(\zeta)$.
Since \[
P(q)=\begin{bmatrix}n-1\\ m-1\end{bmatrix},
\] applying Lemma~3.1 to $P(q)$ gives

\begin{equation}\label{eq:P+zata}
  P(\zeta)=
  \begin{cases}
    0,&c\nmid n,\\[2pt]
    \displaystyle \binom{n/c-1}{m/c-1},&c\mid n.
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}


Next, for each \(d\mid r\) and \(d>1\), consider
$R_d(\zeta).$
It is easy to obtain that the order of \(\zeta^d\) is
\[
c'=\frac{c}{\gcd(c,d)}.
\]
Since \(c\mid m\), \(d\mid r\) and \(r\mid m\), we have
\[
\left.c'\right|\frac{m}{d}.
\]
Applying Lemma~3.1 to \(R_d(\zeta)\)  yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Rd+zata+1}
  R_d(\zeta)=
  \begin{cases}
    0,&c'\nmid \frac nd,\\[2pt]
    \displaystyle \binom{\frac{n/d}{c'}-1}{\frac{m/d}{c'}-1}, & c'\mid \frac nd.
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Obviously, the condition \(c'\mid n/d\) is equivalent to
\[
\left.\frac{c}{\gcd(c,d)}\right| \frac nd
\iff
\operatorname{lcm}(c,d)\mid n.
\]
By \(d\mid r\) and \(r\mid m\), this is further equivalent to \(c\mid n\). Hence, we derive
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Rd+zata+2}
  R_d(\zeta)=
  \begin{cases}
    0,&c\nmid n,\\[2pt]
    \displaystyle \binom{\frac{n}{\operatorname{lcm}(c,d)}-1}{\frac{m}{\operatorname{lcm}(c,d)}-1}, & c\mid n.
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
In particular, when \(c\mid n\), the value \(R_d(\zeta)\) depends only on \(\operatorname{lcm}(c,d)\).

We begin to compute $R(\zeta)$ and claim $R(\zeta)=P(\zeta)$. We arrange the proof of this claim as follows.
Now extend the definition by setting \(R_1(q)=P(q)\) and \(\mu(1)=1\). We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq+mobi+sum}
\sum_{d\mid r}\mu(d)R_d(\zeta)=0.
\end{equation}
If \(c\nmid n\), then (\ref{eq+mobi+sum}) is immediate from (\ref{eq:P+zata}) and (\ref{eq:Rd+zata+2}). So in the following, we suppose \(c\mid n\). Choose a prime \(p\mid c\). Since \(c\mid m\) and \(c\mid n\), we have \(p\mid m\) and \(p\mid n\), hence \(p\mid r\). Note $\mu(d)=0$ for $d$ having a square divisor. So we don't need to consider such case in (\ref{eq+mobi+sum}). For every squarefree divisor \(d\mid r\) with \(p\nmid d\), pair \(d\) with \(d\,p\). Then \(d\,p\mid r\) and
$
\mu(dp)=-\mu(d).
$
Moreover, it follows from \(p\mid c\) that
\[
\operatorname{lcm}(c,dp)=\operatorname{lcm}(c,d),
\]
which combining (\ref{eq:Rd+zata+2}) gives \(R_{dp}(\zeta)=R_d(\zeta)\). Therefore
\[
\mu(d)R_d(\zeta)+\mu(dp)R_{dp}(\zeta)
=
\mu(d)R_d(\zeta)-\mu(d)R_d(\zeta)=0.
\]
In consequence, all terms cancel in pairs, which implies (\ref{eq+mobi+sum}).

From (\ref{eq+mobi+sum}) and the definition of \(R(q)\), we obtain
\[
P(\zeta)-R(\zeta)
=
P(\zeta)+\sum_{\substack{d>1,\, d\mid r}}\mu(d)R_d(\zeta)
=
\sum_{d\mid r}\mu(d)R_d(\zeta)=0.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq+R+P+zata}
R(\zeta)=P(\zeta).
\end{equation}
In what follows we will compute $N(\zeta)$ by considering two cases:


\textbf{Case 1}: \(c\mid n\). Then \(n+1\equiv 1\pmod c\), so
\[
[n+1]_{\zeta}
=
\frac{1-\zeta^{n+1}}{1-\zeta}
=
\frac{1-\zeta}{1-\zeta}=1.
\]
Together with (\ref{eq+R+P+zata}), this yields
\[
N(\zeta)=P(\zeta)-[n+1]_{\zeta}R(\zeta)=P(\zeta)-R(\zeta)=0.
\]


\textbf{Case 2}: \(c\nmid n\). Combining (\ref{eq:P+zata}) and (\ref{eq:Rd+zata+2}) gives \(P(\zeta)=0\) and \(R(\zeta)=0\), so again
\[
N(\zeta)=P(\zeta)-[n+1]_{\zeta}R(\zeta)=0.
\]


Therefore \(N(q)=P(q)-[n+1]_q R(q)\) vanishes at every root of \([m]_q\). Because each root of \([m]_q\) is simple, $Q(q)$ is a polynomial in $q$.
Note for any two polynomials $U(q)$ and $V(q)$ in \(\mathbb{Z}[q]\) that the quotient $U(q)/V(q)$ is in \(\mathbb{Z}[q]\) when $V(q)|U(q)$ and the leading coefficient of $V(q)$ is $1$. In consequence, $Q(q)\in\mathbb{Z}[q].$



Finally, it remains to bound the degree $\deg Q(q)\leq\delta-m+1$. In terms of $Q(q)=N(q)/{[m]_q}$, it suffices to prove $\deg N(q)\leq \delta$.
It follows from $L_d=\delta-n-\deg R_d(q)$ and the nonnegativity of $L_d$ in (\ref{Ld+posi}) that
$
\deg R(q)+n\le \delta
$
for every \(d>1\).
Therefore
$
\deg\bigl([n+1]_q R(q)\bigr)
\le
n+\deg R(q)
\le
\delta.
$
In consequence, we have
\[
\deg N(q)\le \delta.
\]

(ii)
For each $d\mid r$ and $d>1$, let
\begin{eqnarray}\label{def+Wd}
 W_d(q):=\frac{R_d(q)(1-q^{L_d})}{1-q^m}.
\end{eqnarray}
Combining (\ref{def+R}) and (\ref{def+Wd}) immediately implies
\begin{eqnarray}\label{def+Wd+W}
W(q)=\frac{R(q)-S(q)}{1-q^m}
=-\sum_{\substack{d\mid r, d>1}}\mu(d)
\frac{R_d(q)(1-q^{L_d})}{1-q^m}=-\sum_{\substack{d\mid r, d>1 }}\mu(d)W_d(q).
\end{eqnarray}
Obviously, $q^{\delta-n-m}W_d(q^{-1})=W_d(q)$, which by (\ref{def+Wd+W}) immediately gives $q^{\delta-n-m}W(q^{-1})=W(q).$
In the following, in order to prove $W(q)\in\mathbb{Z}[q]$, it suffices to show $W_d(q)\in\mathbb{Z}[q]$.
We can prove this in a similar way with the proof $Q(q)\in\mathbb{Z}[q]$ in terms of the following two cases:


\textbf{Case 1: \(c\nmid n\).}
By Lemma~3.1, we have \(R_d(\zeta)=0\), which by (\ref{def+Wd}) implies $W_d(\zeta)=0$.


\textbf{Case 2: \(c\mid n\).}
Again by Lemma~3.1, \(R_d(\zeta)\neq 0\). We claim that \(c\mid L_d\). Recall that
\[
L_d=\delta-n-\deg R_d,
\]
where
$
\delta=(n-m)(m-1),\deg R_d=\left(\frac md-1\right)(n-m).
$
Thus, we obtain
\[
\delta-\deg R_d
=
(m-1)\bigl(n-m\bigr)-\left(\frac md-1\right)(n-m)
=
\frac{m}{d}(d-1)(n-m).
\]
Obviously, $m/d\in \mathbb{Z}$ by $d|r$ and $r|m$, and \(c\mid n-m\) by \(c\mid m\). Hence, we obtain
\[
L_d=\delta-n-\deg R_d\equiv \delta-\deg R_d\equiv 0\pmod c.
\]
Therefore
$
1-\zeta^{L_d}=0,
$  which implies $W_d(\zeta)=0$.


In consequence, in both cases the numerator \(R_d(q)(1-q^{L_d})\) vanishes at every nontrivial \(m\)-th root of unity. Obviously, it is also true for $q=1$.
So similar to the proof of $Q(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$, we derive $W_d(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$.

This completes the proof.

\label{lem:split}
Let $\lambda$ be a nonempty partition.
Suppose that integers $H$ in (\ref{def:H}) and $h$ satisfy
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 H>1,\quad 0<h<H,\quad H\nmid2h,\quad \lambda_1>2h,\quad H\mid\lambda_i
                  \quad(1\le i\le\ell(\lambda)).
 \end{gathered}
\]
Then $T_h(\lambda)$ uniquely determines the pair $(h,\lambda)$ by an
inverse independent of $H$.

label: ineq:labta
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $T_h(\lambda)=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{\ell(\lambda)+1})$.
(1) We first determine $h$ from the smallest entry of $T_h(\lambda)$.
In terms of the hypotheses conditions, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{ineq:labta}
\lambda_1-h>h,\quad \lambda_i\ge H>h\quad(1\le i\le\ell(\lambda)).
\end{equation}

Since $T_h(\lambda)$ is the decreasing rearrangement of
$(h,\lambda_1-h,\lambda_2,\ldots,
\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)})$, it follows from (\ref{ineq:labta}) that
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mu_1&\ge\cdots\ge\mu_{\ell(\lambda)}>
                 \mu_{\ell(\lambda)+1}=h,\\
 \mu_i&\ge\min\{H,\lambda_1-h\}>h
                 \quad(1\le i\le\ell(\lambda)).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus we obtain $h=\mu_{\ell(\lambda)+1}$. 

(2) In what follows we will determine $\lambda$. To recover $\lambda$, it suffices to delete this
entry $h$ and apply one of the following replacements to the remaining entries before
reordering:
\[
 \begin{cases}
  \mu_1-h\longmapsto\mu_1,
    &\text{if }\mu_j=\mu_1-h
                  \text{ for some }1\le j\le\ell(\lambda),\\
  \mu_1\longmapsto\mu_1+h,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]

Now we verify this rule according to whether the largest entry $\lambda_1$ of
$\lambda$ occurs more than once:

\textbf{Case 1}: If
$\lambda_j=\lambda_1$ for some $2\le j\le\ell(\lambda)$, then
\[
 \mu_1=\lambda_1,\quad
 \mu_1-h=\lambda_1-h,\quad
 \bigl|\{i:1\le i\le\ell(\lambda),\
                      \mu_i=\mu_1-h\}\bigr|=1.
\]
Indeed, $\lambda_1-h$ occurs among
$\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{\ell(\lambda)}$, but
$H\nmid(\lambda_1-h)$ whereas $H\mid\lambda_i$
for $2\le i\le\ell(\lambda)$.
So, the first replacement therefore recovers $\lambda$.

\textbf{Case 2}: If $\ell(\lambda)=1$, or if
$\ell(\lambda)\ge2$ and $\lambda_2<\lambda_1$, then
\[
 \lambda_1-\lambda_i\ge H>h
                \quad(2\le i\le\ell(\lambda)),
 \quad \mu_1=\lambda_1-h.
\]
Moreover, $\mu_1-h=\lambda_1-2h$ and $H\nmid(\mu_1-h)$ because
$H\mid\lambda_1$ and $H\nmid2h$. Since
$\{\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{\ell(\lambda)}\}

we have

head: environment

label: ineq+M
title: Proof
body_md:
By (\ref{def+Rq+new}), for each $k\ge0$, the coefficient of $q^k$ in $R(q)$ is
\begin{eqnarray*}
 R_k&=&
 \sum_{\substack{\lambda\in\mathcal P\\
                  wt(\lambda)=k,\ M(\lambda)>0}}M(\lambda)
 - \sum_{\substack{\lambda\in\mathcal P\\
                  wt(\lambda)=k,\ M(\lambda)<0}}(-M(\lambda))\\
&\geq&\bigl|\{\lambda\in\mathcal P:
       wt(\lambda)=k,\ M(\lambda)=1\}\bigr|
- \sum_{\substack{\lambda\in\mathcal P\\
                  wt(\lambda)=k,\ M(\lambda)<0}}(-M(\lambda)).
\end{eqnarray*}
So in order to show $R(q)\geq_q 0$, it suffices to prove 
\begin{eqnarray}\label{ineq+M}
 \bigl|\{\lambda\in\mathcal P:
       wt(\lambda)=k,\ M(\lambda)=1\}\bigr|
\geq\sum_{\substack{\lambda\in\mathcal P\\
                  wt(\lambda)=k,\ M(\lambda)<0}}-M(\lambda).
\end{eqnarray}


Fix $\lambda\in\mathcal P$ with $M(\lambda)<0$, and set
$c=-M(\lambda)$ and $H=H(\lambda)$. For each such partition with $M(\lambda)<0$, we will use $T_h(\lambda)$ to construct $c$ distinct
partitions $\lambda'$ with $wt(\lambda')=wt(\lambda)$ and $M(\lambda')=1$, with no overlap
between different sources.
Obviously, the partition $\lambda$ is nonempty since $M(\lambda)<0$ and $M(\varnothing)=1$.
Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:multiplicity} (iii) and (iv), $H$ has $s\ge4$ distinct prime
divisors and $c\le2^{s-1}-1$. We first prove the next claim.
\begin{cla}
In terms of $T_h(\lambda)$, at least $c$ choices of the splitting parameter
$h$ are available. 
\end{cla}
\begin{proof}Let $p$ be the smallest prime divisor of $H$ and set
\[
 \mathcal A_\lambda:=
 \{h\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:p\mid h,\ 2h<H,\
                         \gcd(h/p,H/p)=1\}.
\]
In terms of definition of $H$, the integer $H/p$ is odd. Writing $h=pj$, we have
\[|\mathcal A_\lambda|=|\{
 1\le j<\frac{H/p}{2},\quad \gcd(j,H/p)=1.\}|
\]
The units $j$ modulo $H/p$ occur in pairs $j$ and $H/p-j$. Since
$H/p$ is squarefree, this pairing and the product formula for
Euler's totient function give
\[
 |\mathcal A_\lambda|
 =\frac12\prod_{\substack{r\mid H\\r\ne p}}(r-1)
 \ge\frac{2\cdot4\cdot6}{2}\,2^{s-4}
 =3\cdot2^{s-1}>c,
\]
where for the first inequality from the first three primes dividing $H/p$ are at
least $3,5,7$, and every remaining prime contributes a factor of
at least $2$. This proves this claim.
\end{proof}

From this claim, we assume that
$h_1(\lambda)<\cdots<h_c(\lambda)$ are the first $c$ elements of
$\mathcal A_\lambda$. In terms of the definition (\ref{def+M+labta}) of $M(\lambda)$, we next verify that each split
$\nu=T_{h_i(\lambda)}(\lambda)$ belongs to $\mathcal S_p$ and satisfies
$M(\nu)=1$. In order to prove $\nu\in\mathcal S_p$, by (\ref{def+SS}), we need to show that $\ell(\nu)\le m/p-1,\,
       p\mid\nu_i\quad {\text{for}}\quad 1\le i\le\ell(\nu)\}$. Put $h=h_i(\lambda)$. Since $H\mid\lambda_j$ for
$1\le j\le\ell(\lambda)$, we have
\[
 \lambda_1\ge H>2h>0.
\]
Thus $0<h<H$, $\lambda_1>2h$, and $H\nmid2h$, so the conditions of
Lemma~\ref{lem:split} are satisfied. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:split}, we obtain $\lambda'=\nu=T_{h_i(\lambda)}(\lambda)$. The largest entry of $\nu$ is at most
$\lambda_1\le n-m$. Let $\phi$ be the second-smallest prime divisor
of $H$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:multiplicity} (2),
$\ell(\lambda)+1\le m/\phi$, which combines
$p\phi\mid m$ and $\phi>p$ to give
\[
 \frac mp-\frac m\phi=\frac{m}{p\phi}(\phi-p)\ge1,
 \qquad
 \ell(\nu)=\ell(\lambda)+1\le\frac m\phi\le\frac mp-1.
\]
In consequence, $\nu\in\mathcal P$. To compute $H(\nu)$, observe that
\[
 \gcd(r,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{\ell(\lambda)+1})
 =\gcd(r,\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)},h).
\]
Using $rad(\gcd(u,v))=\gcd(rad (u),v)$ for $u,v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}$, we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 H(\nu)
 &=rad\bigl(\gcd(r,\lambda_1,\ldots,
                       \lambda_{\ell(\lambda)},h)\bigr)=\gcd(H,h)=p,
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality follows from $h=p(h/p)$,
$\gcd(h/p,H/p)=1$ and the squarefreeness of $H$. Hence, we obtain
$p\mid H(\nu)$ and $\ell(\nu)\le m/p-1$, so
$\nu\in\mathcal S_p$. Since $H(\nu)=p$,
by \eqref{eq:partition-multiplicity}, we also have $M(\nu)=-\mu(p)=1$.
From the above, we have construct $c$ distinct
partitions $\lambda'$ with $wt(\lambda')=wt(\lambda)$ and $M(\lambda')=1$.


Finally, we show that the resulting partitions are distinct, even
when they arise from different $\lambda$. For every
$\lambda\in\mathcal P$ with $M(\lambda)<0$ and
$1\le i\le-M(\lambda)$, define
\[
 \Phi(\lambda,i):=T_{h_i(\lambda)}(\lambda).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:split}, $\Phi(\lambda,i)$ determines both
$\lambda$ and $h_i(\lambda)$. The increasing order $h_1(\lambda)<\cdots<h_c(\lambda)$ of
$\mathcal A_\lambda$ then determines $i$. Thus $\Phi$ is
injective and preserves weight. So we obtain for every $k\ge0$ that
\[
 \bigl|\{\nu\in\mathcal P:
       wt(\nu)=k,\ M(\nu)=1\}\bigr|
 \ge
 \sum_{\substack{\lambda\in\mathcal P\\
                  wt(\lambda)=k,\ M(\lambda)<0}}(-M(\lambda)),
\]
which implies (\ref{ineq+M}). This completes the proof.

label: prop:domination
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq+M+lanbt+case
title: Proof
body_md:
For each $\lambda\in\mathcal P$ with $M(\lambda)>0$ and each
$i\in[1, M(\lambda)]$, we will construct a nonzero polynomial
\[
 v_{\lambda,i}\in
 V_{m-1,wt(\lambda)}\cap\ker\mathcal D
\]
such that all such assigned polynomials have distinct leading monomials.
The polynomials of any fixed weight will then be linearly independent.
Once the construction is complete, for $0\le k\le\delta/2$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel}, we have

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 C_k
 &=\dim_{\mathbb Q}\ker\bigl(
     \mathcal D:V_{m-1,k}\longrightarrow V_{m-1,k-1}\bigr)\\
 &\ge
   \sum_{\substack{\lambda\in\mathcal P\\wt(\lambda)=k}}
        \max\{M(\lambda),0\}\\
 &\ge
   \sum_{\substack{\lambda\in\mathcal P\\wt(\lambda)=k}}
        M(\lambda)\\
 & =R_k.
 \end{aligned}
\]
It therefore remains to construct such polynomials and distinguish
their leading monomials.

Suppose $m\ne6$. For each partition $\lambda$, we first assign a polynomial in terms of the following rule: For $\lambda=\varnothing$, define
\[
 v_{\lambda,1}:=x_0^{m-1}.
\]
For a nonempty $\lambda\in\mathcal P$ with $M(\lambda)>0$, put
$H=H(\lambda)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:multiplicity} (i), the smallest
prime divisor $p$ of $H$ satisfies
$\ell(\lambda)\le m/p-1$. Moreover,
$H\mid\lambda_j$ and $\lambda_j\ge p\ge2$ for every
$j\in[1,\ell(\lambda)]$. Hence, for $C(\lambda)$ defined in (\ref{def+C+labta}), we have
\[
 \begin{cases}
 C(\lambda)=2\ell(\lambda)\le m-2,&p=2,\\
 C(\lambda)\le3\ell(\lambda)
       \le3(m/p-1)\le m-3,&p\ge3.
 \end{cases}
\]
So, $C(\lambda)\leq m-1$, which satisfies the condition of definition of $C(\lambda)$. Hence we can define a polynomial $K_\lambda$ by (\ref{eq:generl-vector}).  Take $v_{\lambda,1}:=K_\lambda$, and we have
$v_{\lambda,1}\in V_{m-1,wt(\lambda)}\cap\ker\mathcal D$. In addition, its leading monomial is
\[
 x_0^{m-1-\ell(\lambda)}
       \prod_{j=1}^{\ell(\lambda)}x_{\lambda_j},
\]
which is determined by $\lambda$. Therefore, for different $\lambda$, such first polynomials have
distinct leading monomials.

Assume $M(\lambda)\ge2$. In what follows we will assign polynomials to $i\in[2, M(\lambda)]$ additional copies and do it by the following two cases: 

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Case 1.} $H\ne6$.

We first show that there are enough splitting parameters (at least $M(\lambda)-1$). Let $s$
be the number of distinct prime divisors of $H$, and define
\[
 \mathcal A_\lambda
 :=\{h\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:2h<H,\ \gcd(h,H)=1\}.
\]

We have the next claim.
\begin{cla}
\[
 |\mathcal A_\lambda| \ge M(\lambda)-1.
\]
\end{cla}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:multiplicity}(ii) and (iv),
$s\ge2$ and $M(\lambda)\le2^{s-1}$.
Pairing the reduced residues $h$ and $H-h$ gives
\[
 |\mathcal A_\lambda|
 =\frac12\prod_{\substack{q\mid H\\q\text{ prime}}}(q-1)-1
 \ge2^{s-1}-1
 \ge M(\lambda)-1.
\]
Indeed, if $H$ is odd, then every factor $q\geq3$.
If $H$ is even, then one factor $q=2$, but
$H\ne6$ and $s\ge2$ ensure a prime divisor $q\ge5$ and every remaining $q\geq3$.
\end{proof}
Thus, from this calim, we let $h_2(\lambda)<\cdots<h_{M(\lambda)}(\lambda)$ be the first
$M(\lambda)-1$ elements of $\mathcal A_\lambda$. We now verify that each $h_i(\lambda)$ chosen produces an admissible
polynomial. We claim:
\begin{cla}
Fix $i\in[2, M(\lambda)]$ and let $h=h_i(\lambda)$ and $\nu=T_h(\lambda)$ as in
\eqref{eq:partition-split}. Then there exists a $v_{\lambda,i}
 \in V_{m-1,wt(\lambda)}\cap\ker\mathcal D.$
\end{cla}
\begin{proof}
Since
\[
 2\le h\,\, {\text{and}}\,\, 2h<H\le\lambda_1\le n-m,
\]
both $h$ and $\lambda_1-h$ lie in $\{2,\ldots,n-m\}$.
The unchanged entries of $\lambda$ lie in this set as well.
Let $\phi$ be the second-smallest prime divisor of
$H$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:multiplicity}(ii), we obtain
$\ell(\lambda)+1\le m/\phi$. We begin to consider the following two cases:

(i) If $H$ is odd, then $\phi\ge5$ and in terms of the definition (\ref{def+C+labta}) of $C(\lambda)$, we have 
\[
 C(\nu)\le3(\ell(\lambda)+1)
       \le\frac{3m}{\phi}\le m-1.
\]


(ii) If $H$ is even, then the entries of $\lambda$ are even and $h$
is odd. Splitting $\lambda_1$ replaces one even entry by two odd
entries, we obtain
\[
 C(\nu)=2(\ell-1)+3\times2=2\ell(\lambda)+4
       \le\frac{2m}{\phi}+2\le m-1,
\]
where the last inequality follows from the fact: if $\phi=3$, then $6\mid m$ and $m\ne6$
give $m\ge12$; if $\phi\ge5$, then $2\phi\mid m$. 
Also, we obtain
\[
 \ell(\nu)=\ell(\lambda)+1\le m/\phi\le m-1,
 \quad \nu_1\le n-m.
\]
Thus $\nu\in\mathcal P$ and $\nu_1\le n-m$ satisfies the condition of the definition (\ref{def+C+labta}) of $C(\lambda)$. So, by (\ref{eq:generl-vector}), we define  assign
\[
 K_\nu
 \in V_{m-1,wt(\lambda)}\cap\ker\mathcal D.
\]
So we take $v_{\lambda,i}:=K_\nu$. This completes the claim.
\end{proof}

Finally, we show that different $v_{\lambda,i}$ has the different leading monomials, which implies that they are different. Let
$\nu=T_{h_i(\lambda)}(\lambda)$ be an assigned split. Since
$\ell(\nu)=\ell(\lambda)+1$, the leading monomial of $K_\nu$
differs from that of the first-copy polynomial $K_\lambda$.
For a first-copy polynomial indexed by $\lambda'$ ($\ne\lambda$), we have
\[
 H(\nu)
 =rad\bigl(\gcd(r,\lambda_1,\ldots,
                    \lambda_{\ell(\lambda)},h_i(\lambda))\bigr)
 =\gcd(H(\lambda),h_i(\lambda))=1,
\]
whereas $H(\lambda')>1$. The latter follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:multiplicity}(i) when $\lambda'$ is nonempty, and from
$H(\varnothing)=rad (r)>1$ otherwise. Thus a split polynomial has
a different leading monomial from every first-copy polynomial.

For a fixed $\lambda$ and $2\le i<j\le M(\lambda)$, the smallest
entries of $T_{h_i(\lambda)}(\lambda)$ and
$T_{h_j(\lambda)}(\lambda)$ are
$h_i(\lambda)$ and $h_j(\lambda)$, respectively. Since they are distinct,
the corresponding leading monomials are distinct. Finally, splits
arising from distinct source partitions cannot coincide: by
Lemma~\ref{lem:split}, their common image would determine a unique
source partition. Hence all assigned leading monomials are distinct.


\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Case 2.} $H=6$.

We first determine the number of additional copies. Since
$6\mid r$, $r\mid m$ and $m\ne6$, we have $m\ge12$. Formula
\eqref{eq:partition-multiplicity} becomes
\begin{eqnarray}\label{eq+M+lanbt+case}
M(\lambda)
 =\mathbf1_{2(\ell(\lambda)+1)\le m}
  +\mathbf1_{3(\ell(\lambda)+1)\le m}
  -\mathbf1_{6(\ell(\lambda)+1)\le m}.
\end{eqnarray}
It follows from $M(\lambda)\ge2$ and (\ref{eq+M+lanbt+case}) that
\begin{eqnarray}\label{ineq+M+lanbta}
 M(\lambda)=2,\quad
 \frac m6\le\ell(\lambda)\le\frac m3-1.
\end{eqnarray}

In what follows we divide the remaining proof into two cases:


\textbf{Case 2.1}: $\lambda_1\ge12$. So we can use a split. Take $h=5$ and let 
$\nu=T_5(\lambda)$. We have inequalities
\[
 0<h<6,\quad \lambda_1\ge12>2h,\quad 6\nmid 2h.
\]
Obviously, these inequalities satisfy the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem:split}. So, by computing for $H=6$, we have every entry of $\nu$ lies between
$5$ and $n-m$, and
\[
 C(\nu)=2(\ell-1)+2\times 3=2\ell (\lambda)+4
       \le\frac{2m}{3}+2\le m-1,\quad
 \ell(\nu)=\ell(\lambda)+1
       \le\frac m3\le m-1.
\]
Therefore $\nu\in\mathcal P$, and we can define $K_\nu$ by (\ref{eq:generl-vector}). So, taking $v_{\lambda,2}=K_\nu$, we have
\[
 v_{\lambda,2}
 \in V_{m-1,wt(\lambda)}\cap\ker\mathcal D.
\]
Here $H(\nu)=\gcd(6,5)=1$. As in Case~1,
by Lemma~\ref{lem:split}, we distinguish this leading partition from
all other assigned splits.

\textbf{Case 2.2}: $\lambda_1<12$. Since every entry is divisible
by $6$, we have $\lambda=(6^{\ell(\lambda)})$.
As $n-m\ge m\ge12$, we can define $f_6$ and $\Delta$ in (\ref{eq:even-vector}) and (\ref{eq:delta-vector}), respectively.
Set
\[
 v_{\lambda,2}
 :=x_0^{\,m/3-1}
   \Delta^{\,m/3-\ell(\lambda)}
   f_6^{\,2\ell(\lambda)-m/3}.
\]
In the following, we will prove $ v_{\lambda,2}\in \ker\mathcal D $.
The bounds in (\ref{ineq+M+lanbta}) on $\ell(\lambda)$ show that all exponents are
nonnegative integers. From Section~\ref{sec:kernel}, we have
$\mathcal D x_0=\mathcal D\Delta=\mathcal D f_6=0$;
the derivation rule therefore gives
$\mathcal Dv_{\lambda,2}=0$. Moreover,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
\deg( v_{\lambda,2})&= (m/3-1)+4(m/3-\ell(\lambda))
       +2(2\ell(\lambda)-m/3)=m-1,\\
wt( v_{\lambda,2})&= 6(m/3-\ell(\lambda))
       +6(2\ell(\lambda)-m/3)
       =6\ell(\lambda)=wt(\lambda).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
$v_{\lambda,2}\in V_{m-1,wt(\lambda)}$.
Its leading term is
\[
 \operatorname{LT}(v_{\lambda,2})
 =2^{\,2\ell(\lambda)-m/3}
  x_0^{\,2m/3-1}
  x_3^{\,2m/3-2\ell(\lambda)}
  x_6^{\,2\ell(\lambda)-m/3}.
\]
Its leading partition is
\[
 \rho_\lambda
 :=(6^{\,2\ell(\lambda)-m/3},
    3^{\,2m/3-2\ell(\lambda)}).
\]
The multiplicity of $3$ is at least $2$. Moreover,
\[
 \ell(\rho_\lambda)=m/3\le m-1,\quad
 (\rho_\lambda)_1\le6\le n-m.
\]
Thus $\rho_\lambda\in\mathcal P$ and $H(\rho_\lambda)=3$.
Since $3(\ell(\rho_\lambda)+1)=m+3>m$,
By \eqref{eq:partition-multiplicity}, we have
$M(\rho_\lambda)=0$. This leading partition differs from those
of the first polynomials, which have positive multiplicity, and
from those of the split polynomials, which have $H=1$.
Different values of $\ell(\lambda)$ give different multiplicities
of $3$ in $\rho_\lambda$, so these exceptional leading
monomials are distinct as well.

This completes the proof.

label: eq:six-correction
title: Proof
body_md:
We first compute $R(q)$, then obtain a lower bound for $C_k$ from
four summands of \eqref{eq:KOH}. We finish by comparing this bound
with $R_k$ in odd and even degrees.

The hypotheses imply $\gcd(n,m)=6$. In the divisor
formula (\ref{def+R}) for $R(q)$, the divisors greater than $1$ are $2,3,6$, with
M\"obius values $-1,-1,1$, respectively. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:six-correction}
 R(q)=\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n/2-1}{2}_{q^{2}}+[n/3-1]_{q^3}-1.
\end{equation}
For the KOH identity, taking $a=n-6$ and $b=5$ yields
\[
 P(q)={n-1\brack5}={(n-6)+5\brack5}.
\]
We only need to use the four summands of \eqref{eq:KOH} indexed by
$(1^5)$, $(2,1^3)$, $(2,2,1)$, and $(3,1,1)$ to bound $C_k$.
They are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
 \lambda & \text{summand}\\ \hline
 (1^5)   &[5n-29]_{q}\\
 (2,1^3) &q^2[n-7]_{q}[4n-25]_{q}\\
 (2,2,1) &q^4[2n-15]_{q}[3n-21]_{q}\\
 (3,1,1) &q^6{n-8\brack2}[3n-21]_{q}.
\end{array}
\]
For example, if $\lambda=(3,1,1)$, then
$(Y_0,Y_1,Y_2,Y_3,Y_4)=(0,3,4,5,5)$ and
$(\lambda_1-\lambda_2,\lambda_3-\lambda_4)=(2,1)$,
which gives the last row. To compute their contributions to
$C_k$ for $0\le k\le\delta/2$, multiply each summand by $1-q$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (1-q)[5n-29]_{q}
  &=1-q^{5n-29},\\
 (1-q)q^2[n-7]_{q}[4n-25]_{q}
  &=q^2[n-7]_{q}-q^{4n-23}[n-7]_{q},\\
 (1-q)q^4[2n-15]_{q}[3n-21]_{q}
  &=q^4[2n-15]_{q}-q^{3n-17}[2n-15]_{q},\\
 (1-q)q^6{n-8\brack2}[3n-21]_{q}
  &=q^6{n-8\brack2}-q^{3n-15}{n-8\brack2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For these four first differences, their negative terms begin above the range $0\le k\le5(n-6)/2$, since
$n\ge12$ and
\[
 \frac{5(n-6)}2
 <3n-17
 =\min\{5n-29,4n-23,3n-17,3n-15\}.
\]
So we next restrict these four first differences to consider their former terms.
Every remaining summand of \eqref{eq:KOH} has nonnegative first
differences in the same range by the symmetry and unimodality of Gaussian  polynomials. Hnece, for $0\le k\le5(n-6)/2$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:six-bound}
 C_k\ge \mathbf1_{k=0}
  +\mathbf1_{2\le k\le n-6}
  +\mathbf1_{4\le k\le2n-12}
  +[q^{k-6}]{n-8\brack2}.
\end{equation}

We now compare this lower bound with the coefficients of $R(q)$.
By \eqref{eq:six-correction}, $\deg R(q)=2n-12$, so $R_k=0$ for
$k>2n-12$. As the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:six-bound} is
nonnegative, it remains to consider $0\le k\le2n-12$ in terms of the following two cases.

\textbf{Case 1}: For odd $k$, combining \eqref{eq:six-correction} and \eqref{eq:six-bound} gives
\[
 R_k=\mathbf1_{\{3\mid k,\ 1\le k\le n-6\}}
 \le\mathbf1_{2\le k\le n-6}\le C_k.
\]
For the first three even degrees, the same equations give
$c_0\ge1$, $c_2\ge1$, and $c_4\ge2$, while
$(r_0,r_2,r_4)=(1,1,2)$.

\textbf{Case 2}: For the remaining even degrees, write $k=2h$ with
$3\le h\le n-6$. We compute two Gaussian coefficients in
\eqref{eq:six-bound} and \eqref{eq:six-correction} by
\eqref{eq:coeff+Gauss}. In the two counts, the partitions have at most
two parts and are represented by $(2h-6-v,v)$ and $(h-v,v)$,
respectively, with zero parts omitted:
\begin{align*}
 [q^{2h-6}]{n-8\brack2}
 &=\bigl|\{v\in\mathbb Z:\max(0,2h-n+4)\le v\le h-3\}\bigr|\\
 &=\min(h-2,n-h-6)
   &&(3\le h\le n-7),\\
 [q^{2h}]\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{n/2-1}{2}_{q^{2}}
 &=\bigl|\{v\in\mathbb Z:\max(0,h-n/2+3)
                     \le v\le\lfloor h/2\rfloor\}\bigr|\\
 &=\left\lfloor\frac{\min(h,n-h-6)}2\right\rfloor+1
   &&(0\le h\le n-6).
\end{align*}
The second count and \eqref{eq:six-correction} now give
\[
 R_{2h}=\left\lfloor\frac{\min(h,n-h-6)}2\right\rfloor+1
          +\mathbf1_{\{3\mid h,\ 2h\le n-6\}}
 \qquad(3\le h\le n-6).
\]
We compare this formula with \eqref{eq:six-bound} by the following three cases:


\textbf{Case 2.1:} If $3\le h\le n/2-3$, then 
$ C_{2h}\ge h \ge \lfloor h/2\rfloor+1+\mathbf1_{3\mid h}= R_{2h}.$



\textbf{Case 2.2:}  If $n/2-2\le h\le n-7$, then
\[
 C_{2h}\ge n-h-5
 \ge\left\lfloor\frac{n-h-6}{2}\right\rfloor+1
 =R_{2h}.
\]



\textbf{Case 2.3:} If $h=n-6$, then combining \eqref{eq:six-correction} and \eqref{eq:six-bound}
gives $C_{2n-12}\ge1=R_{2n-12}$.


This covers every integer $0\le k\le5(n-6)/2$. The proof is complete.

label: W+rewrite
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall $\delta=(n-m)(m-1)$. Note by Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomiality} that $\deg W(q)=\delta-n-m$. If $\delta-n-m<0$, then the polynomial $W(q)$ must be zeros. If $\delta-n-m=0$, then $m=3$ and $n=9$, or $m=4$ and $n=8$. In this case, it is easy to obtain that $W(q)$ is a nonnegative constant. 
So in the following, we assume $\delta-n-m>0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomiality}, $W(q)=q^{\delta-n-m}W(q^{-1})$.
In consequence, in order to prove $W(q)\ge_q0$, it suffices to show that $[q^k]W(q)$ is nonnegative for $0\leq k\leq (\delta-n-m)/2$.
By (\ref{def+R}), we rewrite
$W(q)$ as
\begin{eqnarray}\label{W+rewrite}
 W(q)=\frac{R(q)}{1-q^m}
 +\sum_{\substack{d\mid r,d>1}}
   \mu(d)\frac{q^{L_d}R_d(q)}{1-q^m}.
\end{eqnarray}
By (\ref{Ld+posi}), we have $L_d\geq0$, where equality holds if and if $d=2$ and $m=4$ for every $d\mid r$ with $d>1$,
\begin{eqnarray}
L_d-\frac{(\delta-n-m)}{2}
 =\frac{m(d-2)(n-m)}{2d}\ge0
\end{eqnarray}
with equality if and only if $d=2$.
Since $R_d(0)=1$, the factor
$q^{L_d}R_d(q)/(1-q^m)$ has the lowest degree $L_d$.
Now we consider nonnegativity of $[q^k]W(q)$ by the following two cases:


\textbf{Case 1}: $0\le k<\frac{\delta-n-m}{2}$.
Combining (\ref{W+rewrite}) and Proposition~\ref{prop:R-positive} gives
\[
 [q^k]W(q)=\sum_{j\ge0}R_{k-jm}\ge0.
\]

\textbf{Case 2}: $k=\frac{\delta-n-m}{2}$.
If $d>2$, then $L_d-\frac{(\delta-n-m)}{2}>0$. Thus, in the second summation of (\ref{W+rewrite}), only the term with $d=2$ contributes in degree $L_2$.
Note $\mu(2)=-1$ and $R_2(0)=1$. It follows from (\ref{W+rewrite}) and Proposition~\ref{prop:R-positive} that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:midpoint-compensation}
 [q^{L_2}]W(q)=\begin{cases}
    \sum_{j\ge0}R_{L_2-jm}\geq0,&2\nmid r,\\[2pt]
    \displaystyle \sum_{j\ge0}R_{L_2-jm}-1\ge R_{L_2}-1,&2\mid r.
  \end{cases} 
\end{equation}
In the following we will prove $R_{L_2}\geq1$.
 
 
 We first consider the case $n-m>6$. Note for every $d\mid r$ with $d\ge3$ that
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 L_2-\deg R_d
 =m(n-m)\left(\frac12-\frac1d\right)-m\ge m\left(\frac{n-m}{6}-1\right)>0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
So the polynomial $R_d(q)$ has no the term $q^{L_2}$ for $d\geq3$.
It follows that $$R_{L_2}=[q^{L_2}]R(q)=[q^{L_2}]R_2(q)=[q^{L_2}]\left.\begin{bmatrix}n/2-1\\ m/2-1\end{bmatrix}\right|_{q\rightarrow q^2}=[q^{L_2/2}]{n/2-1\brackm/2-1}.$$
 By $d=2$, we have $m,n-m\in2\mathbb Z$, which implies $L_2\in 2\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.$ Moreover, we also have
$ 0\le\frac{L_2}{2} \le\deg {n/2-1\brackm/2-1}.$
In consequence, we obtain
\[
R_{L_2}=[q^{L_2/2}]{n/2-1\brackm/2-1}\ge1
\] since the coefficients of Gaussian polynomials are positive integers.


If $n-m\le6$, then $4\le m\le n-m\le6$ and both $m$ and $n-m$
are even. Thus $(n,m)\in\{(8,4),(10,4),(12,6)\}$, and direct
coefficient extraction gives
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 (n,m)&R(q)&L_2&r_{L_2}\\ \hline
  (8,4)&[3]_{q^2}&0&1\\
  (10,4)&[4]_{q^2}&2&1\\
  (12,6)&\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{5}{2}_{q^{2}}+[3]_{q^3}-1&6&3
 \end{array}
\]
In consequence, we have $R_{L_2}\ge1$ and
\eqref{eq:midpoint-compensation} is nonnegative. The proof is complete.

body_md:
From symmetry of Gaussian polynomials, we have $G_{n,m}(q)=G_{n,n-m}(q)$. So it suffices to
consider $3\le m\le n/2$.


If $\gcd(n,m)=1$, then
$G_{n,m}(q)\ge_q0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime}.
So let $r=\gcd(n,m)>1$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction}, in order to prove $G_{n,m}(q)\ge_q0$, it suffices to show
\[
  R(q)\ge_q0,\quad W(q)\ge_q0\quad and \quad C_k-R_k\ge0\quad(0\le k\le\delta/2).
\]  The first two nonnegativity $R(q)\ge_q0$ and $W(q)\ge_q0$ follows from Propositions~\ref{prop:R-positive}
and~\ref{prop:W-positive}, respectively. For the third nonnegativity, it follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:domination} Propostion \ref{prop:domination+m6+2+3} and Proposition~\ref{prop:domination+m6+12}. In consequence, we obtain $G_{n,m}(q)\ge_q0$.

label: eq:m2
title: Proof
body_md:
For $m\ge2$, by \eqref{eq:f-to-g}, we have
\[
 F_{n,m}(q)=G_{n,m}(q)
 \prod_{j=n+2}^{n+m-1}\frac1{1-q^j},
 \qquad
 \frac1{1-q^j}=\sum_{i\ge0}q^{ij}\ge0\qquad(j\ge1).
\]
Hence, if $3\le m\le n-3$, we have $ F_{n,m}(q)\ge_q0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:strong}. The following is the boundary cases:


(i) If $m=n-1\ge2$, then $\gcd(n,m)=1$, so
$F_{n,m}(q)\ge_q0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime}. 

(ii) If $m=1$, then obviously $F_{n,1}(q)=1$.


(iii) If $m=2$ and $n$ is odd, then direct cancellation yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:m2}
 F_{n,2}(q)=G_{n,2}(q)
 =\frac{1-q^{n-1}}{(1-q^2)(1-q^{n+1})}
\end{equation}
whose coefficients are nonnegative by Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime}.


(iv) If $m=n-2$ and $n$ is odd, then $ F_{n,n-2}(q)=G_{n,n-2}(q)=G_{n,2}(q)$. Its coefficients are nonnegative by (iii).
This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:main}.
